paragraphs.source_en: “Meitei was already a braggart in those days.” Having finished his yokan, the master joined the conversation again. “He never once kept a promise. And when anyone reproached him, he never admitted he was wrong; he always dodged the matter with one excuse or another. When the crape myrtles were blooming in that temple precinct, he said he would surely write a great work called An Introduction to Aesthetics before the blossoms fell. I said, ‘Impossible. You could never write such a thing.’ But Meitei answered me, ‘I may not look it, but appearances deceive; I am a man of strong will. If you doubt me so much, let us make a wager.’ I took him seriously, and I believe we settled on a meal at a Western restaurant in Kanda. Though I made the bet because I was sure he would never write the book, inwardly I was still a little uneasy, since I had no money to treat him to Western food. But would you believe it, the fellow showed no sign of beginning; seven days passed, twenty days passed, and he had not written a single page. At last the crape myrtle blossoms fell until not one flower remained. Yet the man himself remained perfectly unconcerned. Thinking I had finally earned my Western meal, I pressed him to honor the agreement, but Meitei, as if nothing at all had happened, simply ignored me.”

paragraphs.source_en: The moment Suzuki heard Meitei mention Kangetsu’s name, he immediately signaled secretly to the master with his chin and his eyes: “Do not speak of Kangetsu, do not speak of him!” But my master never understood his signal at all. When he had just met Suzuki and listened to his reasoning, he had only felt sympathy for Kaneda’s daughter; but now, hearing Meitei say “the Nose, the Nose” again and again, he remembered that earlier quarrel. Remembering it, he found it both comical and, in some measure, the Nose rather hateful. Still, that Kangetsu had begun writing his dissertation was, after all, a good thing; on that point, just as Meitei boasted, it was indeed a rare piece of recent news. Nor was it merely news; it was welcome, pleasant good news. Whether Kangetsu married Kaneda’s daughter or not was of no great consequence; at any rate, it would be excellent for Kangetsu to become a doctor. As for a badly carved wooden image like himself, there was no cause for regret if it were left unfinished in the corner of a Buddhist sculptor’s shop, the bare wood to be eaten by insects; but for a finely carved finished piece, one naturally wishes to see it gilded and brought before the world as soon as possible.

paragraphs.source_zh: 铃木君一听到迷亭提起寒月的名字，便立即利用下颏用眼神暗暗向主人打招呼：“千万不要说寒月的事儿，千万不要说！”但我家主人却始终没明白他的暗号。刚才见面时，听了铃木的一番道理，他只是一味同情金田的女儿，可现在听了迷亭连声“鼻子、鼻子”的，又回忆起从前那段吵架的事儿。一想起这事儿，既觉得滑稽可笑，又觉得那鼻子实在可恨。但是，寒月已开始写作论文，这毕竟是好事儿，这点，倒是的确如迷亭称赞的那样，是近来难得的消息。还不只是消息而已，而且是个令人高兴、令人愉快的好消息。寒月娶不娶金田的女儿，这事儿倒无关紧要，总之，寒月能当上博士是再好不过了。像自己这样雕得不成样子的木像，扔在佛像雕刻店的角落里，那白茬木头任凭虫蛀也无所遗憾；但对于精雕细刻出来的完成品，总希望它能早日涂上金箔早日问世的啊。
